meta.title: Mars Climate Orbiter: the unit mismatch
meta.notes: DEMO. Facts written from general knowledge of the 1999 NASA Mishap Investigation Board report, not extracted from a supplied document: verify against the report before publishing.

scenes.title: Cold open
beats: On September twenty-third, nineteen ninety-nine, a three hundred million dollar spacecraft flew toward Mars, and never came back.
It did not fail because of a broken part, or a bad launch. It failed because two teams used two different units of measurement.

p.title:
The unit mismatch
that sank a probe

scenes.title: The mission
beats: Mars Climate Orbiter launched in December nineteen ninety-eight. Its job was to study the weather on Mars, and to relay signals for a second lander.
The trip took nine and a half months. To stay on course, the navigators at JPL used regular corrections, based on how hard the small thrusters had pushed the spacecraft.
That push is called impulse, and the numbers came from software written by the spacecraft's builder.

scenes.title: The mismatch
beats: The interface document was clear: thruster impulse must be reported in newton-seconds, the metric unit.
But the builder's software produced the numbers in pound-force seconds, the unit used in the United States.
One pound-force second is about four point four five newton-seconds. And nothing in the data said which unit it was.
So the navigators read every number as metric, and every number was off by a factor of four and a half.

scenes.title: Why nobody caught it
beats: The error was small each time. A thruster firing here, a correction there. But the spacecraft fired its thrusters again and again for months.
Each wrong number nudged the predicted path a little further from the real one.
Some team members did notice that the trajectory looked odd. But the concern never became a formal, tracked problem.
The checks looked at whether the software ran, not at what its numbers meant.

banner.text: The checks tested that it ran, not what the numbers meant

scenes.title: The loss
beats: On September twenty-third, the orbiter fired its main engine to enter orbit. By then, the error had piled up.
It was supposed to pass about two hundred twenty-six kilometers above the surface. The real altitude was closer to fifty-seven.
Anything below about eighty kilometers was considered too low for the spacecraft to survive.
Contact was lost as it passed behind Mars, and it was never heard from again.

scenes.title: Takeaways
beats: The lesson is not that engineers made an arithmetic mistake. It is that a number without a unit is only half a fact.
Interfaces between teams need explicit units, checks at the boundary, and a way for a doubt to become a formal problem.
A whole mission was lost to a conversion factor of four point four five.

p.title: What to take away
items: A number without a unit is half a fact
